walkthroughs.body_html:
Urban Environments — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Urban Environments brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Urban Environments.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which African region suffers severe desertification?
options: Sahel
Maghreb
Cape
Horn of Africa

mcqs.q: What is the maximum rainfall in hot deserts?
options: 100mm
250mm
500mm

mcqs.q: Why do informal settlements develop in rapidly growing LIC cities?
options: Because the government forces them to move to cities.
Informal settlements are built by the government for new migrants.
Rural-urban migration outpaces formal housing supply; migrants build their own homes on marginal land without secure land tenure — driven by housing shortage, not by personal choice.
People live in slums because they prefer them or are too lazy to find better housing.

mcqs.q: Why do people move from rural to urban areas in LICs?
options: Informal settlements are built by the government for new migrants.
Because cities in poor countries are always better than the countryside.
Because the government forces them to move to cities.
A combination of push factors (rural poverty, lack of services, agricultural change) and pull factors (perceived jobs, education, healthcare) — though reality often disappoints.

mcqs.q: What is the 'race to the bottom' critique of globalisation?
options: The race to the bottom means TNCs compete with each other for the lowest prices.
Informal settlements are built by the government for new migrants.
Race to the bottom is when companies offshore work to mines and underground factories.

The argument that TNCs play countries off against each other, relocating to those with lowest wages, weakest regulation and lowest taxes — pressuring governments to cut standards to attract investment.
